div.head: Rect 17
div.ab: [17] Be berebrytte. Berebryttan gebyreð corngebrot on hærfeste æt bernes dure, gif him his ealdorman ann, ⁊ he hit mid getryw[ð]an geearnoð.
Berebreto (id est horreario) pertinet habere crodinum ad ostium horrei in Augusto, si aldremannus suus ei concedat, et idem fideliter deseruiat.
Be berebrytte . Berebryttan gebyreð corn gebrot on hær|feste æt bernes dure . gif him his ealdor|man ann 7 he hit mid getrywdan geearnoð .
Be berebrytte Berebryttan gebyreð corngebrot on hærfeste æt bernes dure, gif him his ealdorman ann and he hit mid getrywðan geearnoð.
Vom Getreideverwalter. Dem Getreideaufseher gebührt der Kornabfall in der Ernte am Scheunenthor, wenn [es] ihm sein Vorgesetzter gewährt, indem jener es durch Treue verdient.
Of the granary-keeper. To the granary-keeper is due the spilt grain at the [demesne's] barn door at harvest, if his superior grants [it] to him, and he earns it by faithfulness.
Concerning the barley-keeper To the barley-keeper is due the corn dropped at the barn’s door at harvest, if his overseer grants [it] to him, and he has earned it with diligence.
Regarding the Barley Keeper To the barley keeper is due the grain dropped at the barn door at harvest, if his overseer grants it to him and he has earned it by his diligence.
div.note: The heading ‘berebrytte’ is a Middle English form. B reads ‘getryw[ð]an’ as ‘-wdan’. Liebermann compares Rect 12.

note.seg: Das Wort, bei Toller Suppl. nur hierher, begegnet auch in Somersets. (Warren Leofric missal p. lix) und zu Glastonbury; Neilson Custom. rents 103. Das Wort bere, zunächst ‘Gerste’, heisst ‘Korn’ allgemein in den Compositis bereflor, -tun, -ern, -wic, mengl. -lep (Korb); brytta heisst ‘Verteiler’ [Ein hlafbrytta ‘breadspenser’ (Earle 494) ist ein Unfreier auf einem Gute in Devonshire; vor a. 1000 Bi 1247]. Er verrechnet wohl Eingang des Getreides, Dreschen und Ausfuhr; Andrews 145. Wohl identisch mit späterem gerneter bei Walter Henley ed. Lamond 16 und barnman (jetzt ‘Drescher’ laut Wright Dial. dict.)

The word, in Toller Suppl. only from this passage, also occurs in Somerset (Warren Leofric missal p. lix) and at Glastonbury; Neilson Custom. rents 103. The word bere, primarily ‘barley’, means ‘corn’ in general in the compounds bereflor, -tun, -ern, -wic, ME -lep (basket); brytta means ‘distributor’ [A hlafbrytta ‘breadspenser’ (Earle 494) is an unfree man on an estate in Devonshire; before a. 1000 Bi 1247]. He probably keeps account of the intake of grain, the threshing and the dispatch; Andrews 145. Probably identical with the later gerneter in Walter Henley ed. Lamond 16 and the barnman (now ‘thresher’ according to Wright Dial. dict.)

fragmenta der Vulg. Mat. 15, 37: gebrotu.—Crapinum: ‘palea minutior, beim Schwingen an Korn Abfallendes’, Flandrisch 12. Jh.; crappa: ‘abjectio bladi’ bei Fleta.—Mittelengl. crote ‘Stückchen, Fragment, auch von Brot’, leitet Mätzner her von altfrz. crote, das freilich nur als Kotkugel des Tiermists bezeugt ist, aber nach Diez = Littré von ‘Kloss’ herkommt, also viell. ‘kugliges Stückchen’ bedeutete: daher crodinum?

fragmenta of the Vulg. Mat. 15, 37: gebrotu.—Crapinum: ‘palea minutior, what falls off the corn in winnowing’, Flemish, 12th cent.; crappa: ‘abjectio bladi’ in Fleta.—Middle English crote ‘small piece, fragment, also of bread’ is derived by Mätzner from Old French crote, which, it is true, is attested only as a pellet of animal dung, but which according to Diez = Littré comes from ‘lump’ and so perhaps meant ‘small round piece’: hence crodinum?
